items.title: Germaine Bazzle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006
items.q: And we have many, many, many musicians who started that way, little ones, they say, young men — what’s this child’s name now — Troy Andrews.

ctx.x: No, no, no. You said that very well. My wife and I were in New Orleans just about a year ago. And we were walking I think on Canal Street I guess, and we could hear this sound of this band and we literally followed the sound. And then on the corner of I guess Bourbon Street there was this group of young kids playing. And they were unbelievable. You couldn’t possibly write down what they were playing. And I just thought that was a joy to see, that that still goes on. Is there any organization to that kind of…

I don’t know. Let me put it this way. It’s just that this guy says to this child, “Take this horn and I’m going to teach you how to play this, I’m going to teach you how to play that.” And the little child struggles with it and finally he learns how to play and then you get another kid together. You know it’s coming out of the neighborhoods. It’s coming out of the neighborhoods. And it’s not necessarily that you’re teaching them to read at that point, it’s just teaching them to respond to what’s naturally within.…
Oh, the “Trombone Shorty” they call him.
